title: DDIA 2 · DATA MODELS & QUERY LANGUAGES
subtitle: The shape of your data decides which database fits. Trees of data that are read together (one-to-many) suit documents.
footer: Study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann). Read the book.

blocks.text: Document: a profile is a self-contained tree. One read fetches it all because the data has locality. This works when the data is one-to-many and read as a whole.
Document databases have weak join support, so the join moves into application code. As data gains references, the relational model wins again.

head: Schema-on-write (relational)
Schema-on-read (document)
rows: Static typing: checked at compile time
Dynamic typing: checked at run time
ALTER TABLE + migration (fast in Postgres; MySQL used to copy the whole table)
Just write new docs; code handles both old and new shapes
Heterogeneous items: different shapes per type, or external data you don't control
Rows are spread across tables (but see Postgres JSONB, Spanner interleaving)
Whole doc stored together; rewrites the whole doc on update, so keep docs small
Weak or none; done in application

blocks.text: There is always a schema, it's just implicit in the reading code. You still pay for migrations, just later and in more places.
A recursive query ("WITHIN, any number of hops") is one line in Cypher and painful in SQL (recursive CTE).

blocks.text: "I start from access patterns. The two hot queries are X and Y, and both are key lookups with one join, so Postgres with the right indexes covers it. I'd only move to Cassandra if write volume passes about 50k/sec."
